title: Special agents blood and urine test results stolen in FBI hack
description: Cyber-criminals who hacked the FBI say they have extremely sensitive medical data for thousands of its special agents.BBC News has seen samples of the
body: Cyber-criminals who hacked the FBI say they have extremely sensitive medical data for thousands of its special agents.BBC News has seen samples of the stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations, which contain information such as blood and urine test results, and doctors' notes mentioning conditions such as a "shellfish and banana allergy".The records include agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical concerns including 'blood in the urine' and 'high cholesterol'.Experts say the hack - which the FBI is investigating - could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks, as well as help criminals impersonate law enforcement officers."The list maps thousands of agents against their medical and fitness records," said Etay Maor, vice-president of threat intelligence at Cato Networks."Passwords can be reset if stolen, but medical records cannot, so once this data is out, it stays compromised for good. That permanence, applied across an entire workforce, is what makes this leak so serious."The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday it acknowledged the breach and said it was "aggressively investigating" how it happened.The cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters claims it breached FBI systems on Monday, and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.The group also shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.Unusually, the hackers are not demanding money. Instead, they are seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May, which they claim "offended" them.The samples shared with journalists appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses. The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, has described the hack - if confirmed - "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches."'Phishing, impersonation, identity fraud'The news agency Reuters reports that some of the data includes information on agents, external involved in investigations relating to Russia, China and drug cartels.Reporting by 404 Media suggests details of a previously little-known FBI hacking unit may also have been exposed, external.It was initially thought the breach affected the FBI's 38,000 current employees, but the hackers now claim the number could be far higher.The group says it underestimated the scale of the data theft and now claims to hold sensitive information on around 60,000 current and former FBI staff.Jamie Akhtar, chief executive and co-founder of CyberSmart, said the hackers' claims should be treated with caution but that the breach appeared to be extremely concerning."Such data could be used for highly convincing phishing, impersonation, identity fraud, blackmail or even operations targeting law-enforcement personnel, making the potential implications particularly serious," he said.The hackers, who communicate with reporters in English via the messaging service, Telegram, say they will publish the full dataset in five days unless the FBI meets their demands.ShinyHunters is an international hacking collective that has been active since 2019 and has been linked to a number of high-profile cyber-attacks, including incidents affecting Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas.The group claims it exploited a vulnerability in an Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI, gaining access to multiple platforms including FBIJobs, FBI BEAST, which handles background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which stores medical records, and FBI BICS, which contains investigative information.In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was still trying to determine whether the hackers had breached its systems directly or compromised a third-party provider."We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the statement said.

schema.headline: Special agents blood and urine test results stolen in FBI hack

title: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
description: In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot". "More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania,
body: In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot". "More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life". "As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News. In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded. Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane. Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries. Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

schema.headline: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies

title: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
description: The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.In December 2
body: The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application, external with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case.It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.In a press briefing on Friday, external, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability"."Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms."The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X."The days of censoring Americans online are over."His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.

schema.headline: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X

title: Jay-Z rape accuser formally withdraws allegation
description: A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue.The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming
body: A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue.The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000.The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers.In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever."The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter."I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone."Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations".When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer Beyoncé, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit. She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration.The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee.In a statement to Rolling Stone, external, which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it.He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information."When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story".In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf."Setting out the events that led to her allegation, the woman said she saw an advert on Facebook in September or October 2024 looking for people who might have sexual assault claims against Combs. "The ad triggered memories of being raped when I was 13 years old," she said.She was contacted by a law firm but was not provided with a draft of the lawsuit containing her allegations and did not authorise it before it was filed in October 2024, she said.She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations".She said: "The October Complaint alleges that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me when I was a minor while an unnamed celebrity watched. As discussed above, these allegations were false."Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs. Combs denied Jane Doe's claims, which his lawyer described at the time as one of a number of civil cases "pushed forward by an attorney more focused on media headlines than legal merit".The BBC has contacted Buzbee for comment.In July 2025, Combs was convicted by a criminal court on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends, and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence.

schema.headline: Jay-Z rape accuser formally withdraws allegation

title: Media outlets banned by Trump denied access to White House event despite judge's order
description: CNN and MS NOW reporters say they have been denied entry to cover a White House state dinner despite a judge ruling their access to the grounds must b
body: CNN and MS NOW reporters say they have been denied entry to cover a White House state dinner despite a judge ruling their access to the grounds must be restored.A federal judge said in an overnight ruling that the White House ban on three outlets - CNN and MS NOW and Politico - was likely unconstitutional and that the administration must allow them access, for now. Trump barred them last week, accusing them of "fake news".Journalists with the three outlets were allowed back in on Thursday morning. Then in the evening, a CNN reporter and a producer and an MS NOW reporter said that they were denied entry to cover the guests arriving for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping.The outlets said they had properly submitted their reporters' names for credentials to cover the arrivals.CNN said that about an hour before Xi was scheduled to arrive, the White House said it could cover the event only with a photojournalist and audio technician, but not a team that included a reporter and producer.MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barron-Lopez said she was told by White House staff that she could not be let in, and to contact the White House communications director.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.A White House communications account posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".The incident was the latest in a series of events on Thursday surrounding the ban on some media outlets at the White House.Despite the overnight ruling, CNN, Politico and MS NOW all reported being denied entry to the White House on Thursday morning, prompting a request for an emergency court hearing.In response, the director of White House Operations said in a court filing that the press passes and confiscated badges had been restored by 09:45 local time (13:45 GMT). Shortly afterwards, all three outlets said they were allowed back in.However, networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC, which pulled out in solidarity, have yet to confirm they will resume broadcast coverage from the White House.The chaotic standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Xi to the White House ahead of a state dinner. In his ruling, Judge Timothy Kelly said the ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".He cast doubt on White House claims that the ban was justified in part on national security grounds, pointing out the president made no mention of this in his initial announcement."The record lacks factual support for defendants' contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security," Kelly wrote.Judge Kelly ruled CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in the ban.He ordered the immediate return of the outlets' press passes and a halt to enforcement of the ban for 14 days.In a court filing on Tuesday, the US Department of Justice had accused the news outlets of threatening national security with their coverage. Government lawyers cited stories about missile stockpiles, the construction of the White House ballroom and the recent Republican midterm convention.Trump first announced last Friday he was barring the three outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. By Saturday morning, each outlet reported that they were denied entry to the White House grounds and that their press badges were confiscated. All three outlets accused the Trump administration of violating their constitutional rights.In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".More than 50 media organisations across the ideological spectrum filed an amicus brief in support of the lawsuit, including Fox News, the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal. There have been previous instances of administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a specific press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.But after objections from the other four networks in the press pool, Fox News was allowed in.

schema.headline: Media outlets banned by Trump denied access to White House event despite judge's order

title: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
description: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war c
body: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region. Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

schema.headline: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany

title: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-easte
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026ByNardine SaadRapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made  onstage earlier this month."So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday. The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself.In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now"."What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention." Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done."Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October. US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week.Figure caption, "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at showWhile performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University.After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group. His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well. Sheeran addressed the controversy head-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week. He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

schema.headline: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout

title: Ethiopia war: Internet disrupted in Tigray
description: Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outbreak of fighting this week between regional f
body: Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outbreak of fighting this week between regional forces and the national army.Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray."Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme.The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment.Sources have told the Reuters news agency that the group which controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), ordered the communications blackout, with one suggesting it was to disrupt government drones.The TPLF has not commented.The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.Even before the current disruption, finding video and images to establish what is happening on the ground has been a challenge.So far, other than footage from Mekelle, most of what has been shared online has been from outside the region.Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying.A humanitarian source in the neighbouring region of Afar told the AFP news agency there was "heavy fighting overnight", including drone strikes, around the town of Abala in the mountains between Afar and Tigray, as "federal forces pushed the rebels from entering the town".During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world.  Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions.It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government.On Wednesday, its forces seized control of three airports from federal police.There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in Amhara, as well as Afar.Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.Additional reporting by Peter Mwai, BBC Verify

schema.headline: Ethiopia war: Internet disrupted in Tigray

title: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack
description: It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents.Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon
body: It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents.Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon told the BBC he'd heard whispers that several others have been notified of similar recent breaches by OpenAI agents."Some have chosen to not be public – that's every government's choice on how it wants to handle these things," he said. "The [Australian] government chose a time to release this to gain maximum publicity which is their wont to do."Revealing a data breach can of course be a risky strategy for governments - it leaves them vulnerable to criticism that their security systems aren't up to scratch. But the fact that no sensitive information was leaked put Australia in a stronger position to use the incident."Nobody has died," says the University of Queensland's associate professor Michael Noetel, who studies AI risks. "This is another canary in the coal mine. This sort of loss-of-control incident, even though it's minor now, is what CEOs are worried about getting worse over time."Though Australia has made a name for itself by taking a stand against social media companies, taking up the AI mantle now is another way for Australia to rein in big tech, says Tama Leaver, professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth."It's impossible to say for sure, but it seems incredibly likely that this was very carefully planned."

schema.headline: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack

title: Oleshky: Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
description: Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedByOlga Malche
body: Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedByOlga Malchevska"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.Image source, Maxar Technologies Handout/EPA-EFE/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023.Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive."There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May."I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutionsWhich weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearWarning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below.Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east.Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information."I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety."They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana. Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky.Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish."This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine."If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says.Figure caption, Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone

schema.headline: Oleshky: Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water

title: Students strike across Germany against military service
description: School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.One of the organisers of
body: School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.One of the organisers of the strike, Bela Breitner, from School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service said the federal government was "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service".At one protest in Hamburg, demonstrators waved flags and held up banners emblazoned with the words "We won't take part in your wars".German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made boosting Germany's military a priority following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.A new law introducing voluntary military service came into force in January, with the aim of recruiting volunteers to increase the number of soldiers.However, if the security situation worsens or if too few volunteers come forward, a form of compulsory military service could be considered by Germany's Parliament, the Bundestag.Under the law, all 18-year-olds in Germany are being sent a questionnaire asking if they are interested and willing to join the armed forces.One protester, 16-year-old Elias Bernhard, from Hamburg, said that the responses to the questionnaires "show that young people do not want to join the Bundeswehr [Germany's army]"."That is why I am out on the streets today. That is why we are serious about striking until compulsory military service is off the table. We will carry on."The questionnaire is mandatory for men and voluntary for women. All 18-year-old men will have to take a medical exam to assess their fitness for possible military service.The organisers of the protests, say the trigger came after some 18-year-olds in the northern German towns of Kiel and Flensburg, were sent official invitations for medical exams, even though they expressed no interest in joining the army on their registration forms.The group says over a hundred demonstrations are planned across Germany, including in Kiel, Hamburg, Berlin and Frankfurt.A spokesperson for the Defence Ministry told the BBC that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical examination applies "to all men liable for military service who were born after 31 December 2007".This also applies to people who have stated that they have no interest in compulsory military service. The spokesperson said that since July around 1,000 18-year-old men, who showed no interest in the army, have had the medical exam.During the Cold War, Germany, like many other European countries, had a large army. But it reduced its armed forces during the 1990s after the fall of the Iron Curtain. Germany's former Chancellor, Angela Merkel, ended compulsory military service in 2011.But now, in the face of perceived threats from Russia and heavy pressure from Germany's traditional ally, the US, Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe's strongest conventional army.The Bundeswehr currently has around 186,700 troops. By the early 2030s, Germany wants to raise the number to 260,000, supplemented by around 200,000 reservists, in order to meet new Nato force targets and strengthen Germany's defences.

schema.headline: Students strike across Germany against military service

title: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
description: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any
body: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class. A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school.Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year.Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality."You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition.There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear.The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible. The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf.The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through.Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU.The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently.In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school. In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system.Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching. The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained.The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered.The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law.The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools. Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank.The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren.Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge. "We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said.Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago. The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government".Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals.

schema.headline: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class

title: Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti to build $600m fuel pipeline
description: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has announced that he is helping to fund a new $660m (£500m) fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and DjiboutiThe project
body: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has announced that he is helping to fund a new $660m (£500m) fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and DjiboutiThe project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres.It is expected to begin operations within 18 months.Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one.The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol.Speaking at the ground-breaking ceremony, Dangote, Africa's richest man, said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient.Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction.Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues.The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa.Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day.The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (£1.2bn).In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu.

schema.headline: Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti to build $600m fuel pipeline

title: Angh by Theja Rio at Toronto: The Indian film taking Nagaland to global cinema
description: There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's nort
body: There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's northeastern frontier, and is in Konyak, a tribal language unfamiliar to most Indians, never mind audiences abroad. It was director Theja Rio's first feature and most of its cast faced a camera for the first time.And yet, at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, this quiet film won the Platform Prize, a major juried award.The award is intended to recognise films with a particularly distinctive directorial voice. The jury praised Rio's "refreshing perspective" and the film's portrait of a world rarely encountered on the international screen.The win also gives Angh an unusual route towards the 2027 Academy Awards. Under new rules, winners of designated prizes at six international festivals can qualify for consideration in the International Feature Film category without relying solely on their country's official submission.This does not make Angh an Oscar nominee. But it does place a Konyak-language film from one of India's smallest states inside a global conversation from which such stories have been almost entirely absent.Rio still sounds slightly startled by it. When we speak in Delhi, roughly 72 hours after the win, he has barely had a moment to breathe - Toronto, flights, interviews, more interviews."There were a lot of good films in the competition", he says, including films by far more seasoned directors. His producers were confident. "They thought we were going to win. I wasn't."He is also less solemn than Angh might suggest. Before cinema, he wanted to be a rapper - "a kid from Compton instead of a kid from Nagaland", as he puts it. His tastes still range happily from Black Thought, the lead rapper of American hip-hop group The Roots, to his favourite filmmaker, the Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami.But for his first feature, he turned close to home.Set in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba, the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village, and his young son, as the world around them changes. The Konyaks are one of Nagaland's 17 major tribes, concentrated in the eastern district of Mon, where such chiefs are known as Anghs. Even today, some older men bear facial tattoos associated with the Konyaks' historical practice of headhunting.Anghba and his son are among the last in their region to hold to an ancestral faith as Christianity spreads.Then an American missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall, arrives. The father resists but the son is now curious.Rio says the idea for the film came a few years ago, when he was visiting Mon for another project. What struck him was how closely different generations seemed to live alongside one another there. Within a single family, he says, a grandfather might be a former headhunter, his face still tattooed; two generations later, his grandson might play guitar in a rock band."It feels like you've jumped on a time machine," Rio says. "The past and the present sort of coexist together."The year also matters. Nagaland, which was earlier part of Assam state, formally became an Indian state in December 1963, during a period of profound political and social change. By then, Christianity had been spreading among Naga communities for decades, bringing changes extending beyond religious belief into customs, rituals and everyday life.Dr B Amo Konyak, a scholar of Konyak society, says the changes during this period were almost like a disappearance.Some practices were lost; others "survived in fragments" - in the memories of elders, in family heirlooms. What had once been part of everyday life became heritage.But Dr Konyak says culture did not simply stop. People carried parts of it into new religious and social worlds. Traditions survived, but changed meaning as they changed form.It's this moment of transition that Rio wanted to capture. "The past 50 or 60 years have brought extraordinary churn," he says, widening the distance between generations.In Angh, he explores this through the relationship between the father and son who "intimately love and care about each other very deeply", even as their worlds begin to pull apart.Critic Siddhant Adlakha was struck by the ambiguity the film captures. "Progress and tradition can be nonlinear, even entwined," he says, "rather than strictly opposing forces."The film is yet to reach a wider audience, but its brief trailer offers a glimpse of how Rio constructed this world. Mist hangs over steep green hills; figures move through forests and village paths; fire and lamplight pick faces out of the darkness. The landscape is beautiful but not merely picturesque - a small world held together by ritual, family and geography, while something larger presses in from beyond its edges.Adlakha singles out the quiet close-ups of Anghlong Konyak, the first-time actor who plays the chief, and the "gentleness" with which Rio captures his "subdued rage".What the camera saw mattered almost as much as where it was looking from.Konyak people have long been viewed from the outside. Dr Konyak points to explorers, colonial officials, missionaries and photographers drawn to tattooed faces, ornaments, weapons and headhunting, while the lives behind them often receded from view.Rio was conscious of inheriting that history. "There have been several films and documentaries made about Nagaland," he says, "but these sort of films tend to follow the gaze of the explorer rather than the subject."With Angh, he wanted to reverse that gaze, asking viewers to "step inside the shoes of these characters".The change is subtle but consequential. The Konyaks are no longer an exotic remnant of the past, but people living through what Dr Konyak describes as "love, grief, conflict, faith, uncertainty and generational change".Konyak advisers worked on dialogue, costume and production design, and much of the cast was drawn from first-time Konyak performers. The forest, too, belongs to the people moving through it. Adlakha says Rio treats it "not just as a setting, but as a home with a history", much as an urban filmmaker might treat Mumbai or New York.Rio and cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz shot Angh on 16mm film, drawing on photographs and footage of missionaries and Naga communities from the 1950s and 60s. They wanted to recreate the grain, texture and atmosphere of those archival images, while shifting the point of view from outsider to subject.It was an evocative choice - and a logistical headache. Unlike digital footage, the exposed film could not simply be reviewed on set. Every four or five days, the cans had to be sent to Mumbai for processing, while the crew carried on shooting without knowing exactly what they had captured.There were more prosaic problems too.During a night shoot with Henshall, an old Second World War Jeep was supposed to be driven into frame. It behaved perfectly through rehearsals. But when the cameras began rolling, the engine refused to start. After repeated attempts, the crew managed to capture just one take of the Jeep entering the frame."It was a very difficult night," Rio says.Angh may be Rio's first feature, but its journey places it within a widening map of Indian cinema, especially in the northeast.Adlakha points to filmmakers such as Assam's Rima Das and Meghalaya's Dominic Sangma whose work, he says, reveals "how complex and multifaceted the idea of Indian cinema happens to be".Rio thinks Nagaland still remains at the edge of that scene. Its film industry is, as he puts it, "at a very nascent stage", with little of the reach enjoyed by India's established filmmaking centres.But he hopes some of the attention around Angh travels back with it.There are, he says, "so many talented filmmakers with so many beautiful stories that are yet to be told".For now, though, Rio is looking forward to something more ordinary - getting back to Nagaland."I want to play football with my friends."

schema.headline: Angh by Theja Rio at Toronto: The Indian film taking Nagaland to global cinema

title: Netanyahu defends Israeli military action as delegates walk out before UN speech
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a s
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly. After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice."In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now."The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland".He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians.Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military.The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because he had been denied a US entry visa.Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him."They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said.Netanyahu also accused the media of misrepresenting violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank and said "maybe two or three" people are killed a year.But, according to figures published by the UN, 23 Palestinians have been killed in the context of settler attacks this year - and 72 since the beginning of 2023.Netanyahu went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas.Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity".Netanyahu's comments drew a sharp response from the Turkish presidency's communications director Burhanettin Duran.The Israeli PM's use of the UN General Assembly podium to level "baseless accusations" against Turkey and Erdogan was incompatible with the UN's "ideals of peace, law and dialogue", Duran said, according to state-run news agency Anadolu. New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader."Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said.In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians".Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February."Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said.Much of Netanyahu's speech was pitched at the two audiences he needs to convince the most: Israelis as he faces a critical election at home next month, and Americans as Israel faces growing isolation and fractures in support abroad. In Israel, Netanyahu's once unrivalled image as "Mr Security" has come under increasing scrutiny in what is the first election since the 7 October 2023 attacks. Some political opponents have argued he is unfit for office following Israeli media reports, firmly denied by Netanyahu, that he did not heed warnings of a potential attack by Hamas. His characteristic defiance at the UN podium will be replayed in a campaign seeing his religious-right wing coalition trailing in the polls. Netanyahu appeared to have pre-scripted his comments about "moral cowards" as he faced a mass walkout. It will likely be used as he tries once again to burnish an image as being the only Israeli politician that can truly take on Israel's growing number of global critics. There were also clearly marked references meant for American audiences, including the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran and his praise for Trump. Netanyahu, who was born in Israel but spent his formative years in Pennsylvania, has always tried to present himself as having a unique ability to pitch Israel's case in the US. Despite continued weapons supply from Washington, he faces an increasingly sceptical public. Polls suggest plummeting support for Israel among Democrats, and a fracture in historically high levels of backing among Republicans which has spread to Trump's Maga base.

schema.headline: Netanyahu defends Israeli military action as delegates walk out before UN speech
